newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: Britain's Rifkind warns Iraq against aggression.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Rifkind warns Iraq against aggression.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Monday Iraqi ruler Saddam Hussein had to be taught that new aggression would not be tolerated and called for a new Middle East body to help reduce conflict in the area.

Speaking in Abu Dhabi a day after a hectic round of talks with Israeli and Palestinian leaders designed to give new impetus to the Middle East peace process, Rifkind said Britain was ready to respond again to any threat by Saddam on neighbouring states like Kuwait.
"We have to show Saddam Hussein that any aggressive military adventures, not least when spiced with a well-documented history of brutal repression, are not cost-free.

"If the international community let him throw his weight about in one area, unchallenged, he will surely challenge elsewhere, and the victims will all too likely be among his neighbours. Saddam must be contained," Rifkind said in a speech to businessmen and policy-makers.
But Rifkind said the international community would be ready to help the people of Iraq if their government changed.
"It is, of course, for the Iraqi people to decide how Iraq should be governed," Rifkind said in his speech, which was made available in advance to journalists.

"But I look forward to the day when Iraq is no longer governed by a regime which ignores international obligations and brutalises its own people...Such an Iraq would need the support of the international community to rebuild, to repair the damage of years of misrule."

Rifkind's speech, in which he also criticised Iran for what he described as its "connection with terrorism", was designed to convince the United Arab Emirates of the justification of allied strikes on Iraqi radar installations earlier this year, action which the UAE leaders did not support.
But he also used the speech to launch a British initiative intended to try to prevent conflicts in the region escalating.

"What is lacking at present is an overall structure to encourage cooperation between all the countries of the region with the help and participation of friends outside, like Britain, France, the United States and others," he said.
The body, which Rifkind suggested could be called the Organisation for Cooperation in the Middle East (OCME), would "provide a framework for dialogue and active collaboration.
"It would help to lower barriers and improve links, it would help investment promotion agreements. Its precise priorities would be for its participants to decide," Rifkind said.

Based on the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) rather than a military alliance, the new group could include Turkey, and would eventually be open to countries like Iraq and Iran, said Rifkind. He said he had already floated the idea with countries in the region and other allies like the United States, with a favourable response.
Senior officials travelling with Rifkind said the idea was not designed to replace the Middle East peace process, but to prevent another such crisis erupting.
